executive_summary: AUD/NZD closed at 1.24897 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in New Zealand dollars per Australian dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger Australian dollar. It is up 0.99% over one month, 4.50% over three months, 2.90% over six months and 8.14% over one year, and sits at the 96th percentile of its 52-week closing range, 1.23% above its 50-day average and 11.7% above its 200-week average. The dominant event was 28 October, when Australia's hot September CPI and the RBNZ's surprise 4-3 hold arrived within half an hour of each other. The kiwi fell as much as 1.9% against the Aussie, its largest intraday drop since October 2017, reaching NZ$1.2603 per Aussie, a level last seen in March 2013. The bilateral edge is timing rather than level. The policy gap is 185bp and becomes 210bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November, the RBNZ cannot respond before 9 December, and a rolled long position earns about 183bp a year, roughly 19 pips a month. The two currency views point the same way only tactically. The kiwi-side view favours buying AUD/NZD on dips. The Australian-side view favours selling it strategically, citing the cross's position in its range and a December RBNZ hike, but that hike is already about 76% priced, and our edge is that the RBNZ's 9 December track undershoots what is priced. The tactical stance is Bullish at conviction 3 (score +0.2382), with a base case of 1.2620 by 27 November, entries at 1.2450-1.2490 and a daily-close stop below 1.2330. The strategic stance is Bullish at conviction 2 (score +0.1403), with a base case of 1.2650 by 30 April 2027 plus about 114 pips of carry. There are three caveats. Every located bank forecast sits below spot. New Zealand's Q3 labour data on 4 November is the single largest risk to the call. And Australia's iron ore-driven terms-of-trade loss is the one structural factor scored against the pair.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On World Bank 2025 PPP conversion factors, AUD/NZD fair value is about 1.0529, so spot is 18.6% rich to PPP. The two real effective exchange rates have moved apart over the past year: Australia's BIS real broad index rose 8.77 points to 116.13 in September, while New Zealand's fell 2.07 points to 100.15. That is roughly a 10.8-point relative real appreciation of the Australian dollar, much of it now captured in the cross. History says the level is rare. A 2025 BofA note found that from late November 2013 AUD/NZD had closed at or above 1.12 in only 18 of 614 weeks, about 2.9% of the time. Spot is now 13 big figures above that line and at its highest since 2013. The current level prices the full RBA-RBNZ divergence created on 28 October, but not a downward revision to the RBNZ's own track. Valuation is a strategic headwind that works over years, not inside a six-month window, and it is why the downside scenario is wider than the upside. (52-week intraday range 1.14009-1.26029, spot at the 91st percentile; on closing prices the range is 1.14131-1.2539 and spot is at the 96th percentile, 49 pips below the 28 October closing high and 1,077 pips above the 52-week closing low.)

Scaled by open interest both shorts are near 40-45%, so the cross-implied position is close to flat: speculators are short the Antipodean bloc rather than positioned in AUD/NZD itself. Leg risk reversals are near-identical (-0.885 vols AUD/USD, -0.90 NZD/USD at one month), so hedging demand does not tilt the cross either. The crowding risk specific to this pair is asymmetric: the kiwi short sits in the thinner market and has tighter, data-dated triggers (4 November labour, 7 November election), so a squeeze there would push the pair lower faster than an Australian squeeze would lift it.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Policy differential is RBA 4.60% minus RBNZ 2.75% = +185bp, or +210bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November. Futures-implied carry is 183bp annualised (December 2026 to March 2027 CME AUD/NZD calendar spread, -182.6bp, observed 29 October), which is what a rolled long actually earns and combines the interest differential with any cross-currency basis. The 2-year yield spread is about +113bp (Australia 4.93% on 30 October vs New Zealand 3.80% on 29 October); the live 10-year spread is about +24bp (5.137% vs 4.90%), with September monthly averages of 5.283% vs 4.94% (+34.3bp). Carry-to-vol is 0.27 on the 6.716% estimated three-month implied (a ceiling because the volatility estimate runs low), 0.32 on 60-day realised and 0.24 on 20-day realised. The regime is working: the pair gained 4.50% over three months on top of carry and 8.14% over a year. Carry is meaningful for this cross because realised volatility is low relative to either leg against the US dollar, and a long position is paid to wait through the 3-9 November event cluster, so entry timing matters less than for most crosses. The carry-to-vol ratio of 0.24-0.32 is below AUD/CHF (0.652) and AUD/JPY (0.458) on the Australian-side measures, but AUD/NZD carries far less global equity beta.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Adjusted from the 0.24 default on both horizons. The 185bp policy gap is this cross's defining fundamental, and the timing difference between the two banks is the main thing that sets this pair apart from either currency against the US dollar. An RBA hike on 3 November would take the gap past 200bp, and the framework suggests boosting this factor for high-carry pairs.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy gap is 185bp. The RBA Cash Rate Target is 4.60%, last raised on 29 September by a 9-0 vote. The RBNZ OCR is 2.75%, held on 28 October by 4-3 when markets had heavily priced a hike. The four weeks ahead are lopsided by calendar. The RBA decides on 3 November, with a 25bp hike to 4.85% priced at roughly 79-88% across reports, which would widen the gap to 210bp. The RBNZ does not decide again until 9 December, after the window closes. So no scheduled event in the window can narrow the gap. New Zealand's Q3 labour data on 4 November can only move pricing of the December hike, now about 76%, which the New Zealand-side view puts nearer 60%. Front-end yields tell the same story: the Australian 2-year at 4.93% is about 113bp above the New Zealand 2-year at 3.80%, while 10-year yields are only about 24bp apart, so the Australian advantage sits where policy expectations are priced. The effect reaches the pair through relative short-rate expectations and carry. A rolled futures position currently earns about 183bp a year. Because most of the RBA move is already priced, the remaining surprise is small, and that is why confidence is only in the mid-50s.

tactical.what_is_priced: Most of the 3 November RBA hike is priced (79-88%), as is about 76% of a 9 December RBNZ hike. The unpriced edge over four weeks is the 12-21% of the RBA move still open, plus any trimming of RBNZ December pricing on the 4 November labour data. Both point the same way for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, what matters is how far the gap narrows compared with what is priced. Markets have the RBA adding at most one more hike by about mid-2027 after November. They have the RBNZ resuming at its 9 December decision, which comes with a Monetary Policy Statement, and heading toward a peak that early-October swaps put near 4.1% by December 2027. StoneX reported that the 28 October hold stripped about one full hike out of the New Zealand path by mid-2027, but still judged that traders may be overestimating how much tightening will be delivered. The Australian-side view is a 4.85% peak, with a 35% chance of 5.10% by March. The New Zealand-side view is 3.00% in December and 3.25% by March, with a 3.25-3.50% peak. On those paths the gap is 160bp after a December RBNZ hike and 135-160bp into early 2027. That is wider than the roughly 113bp 2-year spread, which averages expected policy over two years, implies. The scheduled tests are the RBA decisions on 8 December and 9 February and the RBNZ Monetary Policy Review on 10 February. The main risk is on the Australian side. Unemployment has risen three months running to 4.7%, and an RBA pivot that this forces would narrow the gap from the Australian end, which is why confidence is only 52.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish on both horizons. Confidence falls from 55 to 52 because the tactical case rests on a calendar where only the RBA can act, while the strategic case rests on a forecast that the RBNZ will deliver less than priced, which has more ways to go wrong, including an RBA pivot driven by the labour market.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Inflation is higher and broader in Australia. September monthly CPI was 4.3%, and the September-quarter trimmed mean was 3.7%, against the RBA's 2-3% band. New Zealand's Q3 headline CPI was 3.7%, with the 30% trimmed mean at 3.0% and non-tradables at 3.3%, against a 1-3% band. Core inflation is therefore about 70bp higher in Australia, which supports the higher Australian policy rate. Growth momentum cuts the other way. Australian employment fell 39,300 in September, unemployment rose for a third month to 4.7%, and the October flash composite PMI fell to 47.7. New Zealand unemployment was 5.6% in Q2, a decade high, and Westpac expects 5.5% in the Q3 release on 4 November. Over the next four weeks the data come from both sides: New Zealand labour on 4 November, the Australian Wage Price Index on 18 November and the October labour force that week, and Australian October CPI on 25 November. A firm New Zealand print and a weak Australian one would both push the pair lower, while the reverse would push it higher. With no clear asymmetry, the factor is Neutral.

tactical.what_is_priced: Pricing already reflects Australia's hotter inflation through an RBA hike that is 79-88% priced. Pricing for New Zealand assumes the labour market is not deteriorating. Neither economy's growth weakness is fully priced, and that roughly offsets in the cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both economies face the same cost-push fuel shock, but the two central banks are reacting differently. The RBNZ projects New Zealand CPI rising to 4.4% in the December quarter on fuel. Its October majority said indirect fuel effects had been smaller than expected and that weak household spending limits pass-through, which signals it will look through much of the rise. The RBA has been hiking into a similar shock, and Governor Bullock has said inflation is far too high. That reaction difference supports the pair, but it is already captured under Policy and under Guidance. On the growth side, Australia's labour market is deteriorating fastest at the margin. The Australian-side view has unemployment reaching 4.9% by February with real wages falling. New Zealand already carries a saving rate of 3.7% and slack near 5.5%. So the growth argument for an Australian policy peak is building faster than the New Zealand one, and that partly offsets Australia's higher core inflation. The mix is balanced, so the factor stays Neutral at slightly lower confidence.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral on both horizons, at 50 tactically and 48 strategically. The data releases on both sides offset over four weeks, and over the longer horizon Australia's faster labour-market deterioration offsets its higher core inflation.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Global risk appetite is softening at the margin. The VIX was 17.2 on 29 October and the US high-yield spread had widened 18bp in a month to 326bp, but both currencies are high-beta, so the cross moves only on the difference in beta to the shock. The Australian dollar is more exposed to China and iron ore, and China's October manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3. A China-led shock would therefore push AUD/NZD lower. New Zealand is a pure oil importer with thinner liquidity, and NZD/USD has shown a -0.27 correlation with VIX changes over 60 sessions (flagged estimate). A Gulf escalation after the 3 November US midterms would therefore hit the kiwi harder through both fuel costs and risk premia, pushing the pair higher. The two most likely shocks in the window point in opposite directions for the cross, so the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk regime is two-sided for the cross. A Gulf settlement would cut oil and lift equities. That helps both legs, but probably the kiwi more, because it removes New Zealand's largest import-price shock, so it would push the pair lower. Persistent disruption favours Australia, which exports LNG and coal. A global slowdown led by China and AI capital spending would hit the Australian dollar's iron ore and China exposure harder, also pushing the pair lower. Australian superannuation funds' hedging tends to amplify whatever equity regime prevails rather than set the direction. With settlement and slowdown both tilting the pair lower, persistence tilting it higher, and no path dominant, the factor carries no directional signal.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, positioning in each leg is a cushion against further weakness against the US dollar rather than a driver of the cross. Both shorts were built on the same theme, a terms-of-trade and oil shock to commodity-currency importers, and both are near multi-year extremes, so few marginal sellers remain on either side. Australian asset-manager shorts double as hedges of Australian assets and as a funding leg, while the kiwi short is more real-money underweighting. Japanese real-money demand for Australian bonds, at about 237bp over JGBs, slightly favours the Australian leg, as does the steady flow of bank dividends from New Zealand to Australia, but both are slow. The most likely unwind catalysts sit on both sides of the Tasman: a 9 December RBNZ hike that confirms tightening would cover kiwi shorts, and a Gulf settlement would cover both. Without a measurable crowding gap between the legs, the factor stays Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two external positions are similar in size but differ in composition. Australia's current-account deficit reached a record A$27.2bn in the June quarter, 3.67% of GDP. New Zealand's is 3.26% of GDP, with a Q2 deficit of NZ$1.67bn that came in better than expected. The commodity netting is three-way. Oil prices are high, with Brent's expiring front-month contract at $117.64, and that hurts New Zealand, a pure fuel importer, more than Australia, whose LNG and coal exports partly offset its fuel bill. That supports the pair. Against it, iron ore is near $90.60 a tonne after a two-year low, which is a direct Australian terms-of-trade loss, while dairy is firming: the GDT index rose 2.5% on 20 October and Fonterra's midpoint is $9.50/kgMS. Direct bilateral goods trade is modest but tilted toward Australia: Australia exported $8.3bn of goods to New Zealand in 2024 and imported $5.3bn, a $3.0bn surplus. In the window, Australia's September trade on 5 November and New Zealand's October trade on 18 November are expected to confirm each country's own drag. Oil supports the pair while iron ore and dairy weigh on it, so the factor is Neutral over four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the external balance leans against the pair. Australia's terms-of-trade problem looks structural. Iron ore is about 35% of export revenue, Chinese hot-metal output is at its lowest since March, and the Simandou ramp-up adds high-grade supply, so the Australian-side view is $82-90 a tonne by the March quarter. A record current-account deficit built before iron ore fell implies the 1 December balance of payments will show it wider still. New Zealand's problem is mostly oil. The Brent curve is backwardated, so fuel import costs should ease over time even without a settlement. Dairy is recovering, with two GDT gains in October and Fonterra lifting its midpoint from $9.25 to $9.50. New Zealand's 3.26% deficit is also about half its historical 5-7% range. Persistent Gulf disruption is the main offset, because it keeps hurting New Zealand more than Australia. On balance, a structural Australian commodity loss against a partly cyclical New Zealand one tilts the factor Bearish for the pair.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Australia: iron ore (about 35% of export revenue), coal and LNG exporter, net importer of refined fuel. Iron ore up is strongly AUD-positive; oil up is mildly AUD-positive overall because LNG and coal prices partly offset the fuel bill.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: New Zealand: dairy is the dominant export (GDT, Fonterra milk price), and New Zealand is a pure fuel importer with no energy exports. Dairy up is strongly NZD-positive; oil up is NZD-negative through the terms of trade and the trade deficit.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Oil up: Australia mildly positive (+), New Zealand negative (-), so the pair rises. Iron ore up: Australia strongly positive (++), little effect on New Zealand, so the pair rises; iron ore down, as now near $90.60/t, makes the pair fall. Dairy up: New Zealand strongly positive (++), little effect on Australia, so the pair falls. Today's mix of high oil, weak iron ore and firming dairy nets to roughly zero over four weeks: oil supports the pair while iron ore and dairy weigh on it. Over a quarter, a backwardated oil curve, a structurally soft iron ore outlook and recovering dairy all lean against the pair.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair higher. New Zealand's import bill and terms of trade deteriorate with no energy-export offset, while Australia's LNG and coal receipts partly cushion its fuel bill.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair lower. New Zealand's import-price shock eases faster than Australia's, and a lower oil price tied to a Gulf settlement would also lift risk appetite, which helps the thinner kiwi most.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Iron ore over the strategic horizon, because it is the structural Australian loss. Oil is the swing factor tactically, because escalation or settlement in the Gulf moves New Zealand's terms of trade most.

The two banks' communication is diverging sharply, a unanimous and hawkish RBA against a 4-3 RBNZ whose Governor and one majority member disagree on December. The RBNZ track due at its 9 December Monetary Policy Statement is the variable most likely to reprice this cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two banks diverge clearly on communication. The RBA voted 9-0 on 29 September, said it would raise the cash rate further if needed, and Deputy Governor Hauser later said the inflation outlook was significantly worse than forecast. After the 28 October CPI, Governor Bullock said inflation was far too high and likely to exceed the August forecasts. The RBNZ, by contrast, held 4-3 on 28 October. Three members voted to hike. Governor Breman then called a December hike likely, while Hansen, part of the majority, described it as 50-50. StoneX noted this was the RBNZ's second dovish surprise in a row. The RBNZ publishes no further statement, track or minutes before 9 December. The RBA decides on 3 November, though no projection round is flagged for that decision on the published calendar used here. A coherent, hawkish RBA set against a divided RBNZ with no scheduled communication in the window tilts guidance in the pair's favour. The market has already priced much of the hawkish RBA reading, so confidence is modest.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the order of events matters. The RBNZ's 9 December Monetary Policy Statement comes first and will publish a new OCR track. The September track implied only one more hike by year-end, within a 3-3.5% neutral range, and the October majority stressed weak household spending. The New Zealand-side view expects the December track to peak at 3.25-3.50%, below a market path that, even after the hold, StoneX judged may overestimate how much tightening will be delivered. If the election on 7 November produces a Labour-led government, Westpac expects a push to restore a dual inflation-employment mandate for the RBNZ, which would make its reaction function softer. The RBA's credibility has been rebuilt by delivering four hikes in 2026. Its next shift, toward a neutral bias that the Australian-side view expects by February, would weigh on the pair, but its 9 February decision comes a day before the RBNZ's 10 February Monetary Policy Review. The most likely guidance surprise in the window is a New Zealand track below pricing, so the factor stays Bullish at modest confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk in the window falls unevenly on the kiwi. New Zealand votes on Saturday 7 November. The 21-25 October 1News-Verian poll had National on 29% and Labour on 27%, which projects the governing coalition to 61 seats only if the overhang stays small. The New Zealand-side view puts a hung or delayed result, pending special votes in late November, at 40%. A Labour-led government would bring a broader tax base, more infrastructure borrowing and a likely dual mandate for the RBNZ, all kiwi-negative at the margin. Australia has no federal election due before 2028. The US midterms on 3 November open a window for a US strike on Iran, which the New Zealand-side view puts at 25% within four weeks. That would hurt the oil-importing kiwi more than Australia, which exports energy. The upside tail for the kiwi is a Gulf ceasefire, at about 15%. The asymmetry favours the pair.

A returned coalition keeps fiscal consolidation and the reduced NZ$30bn bond programme, which is mildly kiwi-positive. In the Gulf, persistent disruption favours Australia, while a settlement, about 25-30% likely by April, would help the kiwi more through oil. Chinese policy events, the December Central Economic Work Conference and the March National People's Congress, are upside risks mainly for the Australian dollar, but they have under-delivered for iron ore in 2026. With the domestic political tail leaning one way and the largest external tail the other, the factor is Neutral.

There is no fiscal event for either country inside the window, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding conditions are firm rather than stressed, and they affect both legs in similar ways. Year-end dollar demand typically hits the less liquid currency harder, which gives the pair a slight tailwind, but the effect is small relative to the shared exposure. The 9 December FOMC falls on the same day as the RBNZ decision, so dollar news and kiwi news will be hard to separate then. The factor is Neutral.

tactical.score_interpretation: A score of +0.2382 is Bullish, but it rests on depth in one theme rather than breadth. Three factors carry all of it. Two of them, Policy and Guidance, express the same RBA-RBNZ divergence, and none of the three has confidence above 55. No factor is Bearish. At default weights the score would be +0.1954, still Bullish, so the call does not depend on the weight changes. If the theme fails, for example through a strong New Zealand labour print on 4 November, both main contributors would fall together. Mapping to conviction: a score at or above +0.10 maps mechanically to Bullish. Conviction 3 is the judgement attached to that stance.
tactical.rationale: At the applied weights, Policy and Rates (0.28) dominates with +0.154. Guidance (+0.0572) and Event Risk (+0.027) add to it, and the other seven factors score zero, for a net of +0.2382, a Bullish tactical stance. The two currency views reinforce rather than conflict. The Australian dollar is Neutral with a bullish tilt against the US dollar, and the kiwi is Bearish against it, so both point to a higher cross. The bilateral driver neither view fully captures is timing. The RBA decides on 3 November, with a hike to 4.85% priced at roughly 79-88%, while the RBNZ cannot act until 9 December, so nothing scheduled in the four weeks can narrow a 185bp gap that may widen to 210bp. What is priced is most of the RBA hike and about 76% of a December RBNZ hike. The edge we expect is in New Zealand pricing: a split 4-3 committee, a Governor and a majority member who disagree on December, and two dovish surprises in a row make downward revisions to RBNZ expectations likelier than upward ones before December. Event risk falls on the kiwi side. The 7 November election carries a 40% chance of a hung or delayed result and a possible change of government that would soften the RBNZ mandate, while Australia has no domestic political event. The commodity mix is balanced over four weeks: high oil hurts New Zealand, while weak iron ore and firming dairy hurt Australia. The path of least resistance is for the pair to rise on carry of about 183bp a year while RBNZ pricing is tested, interrupted by kiwi-short squeezes around the data. The dated catalysts are the RBA and the GDT auction on 3 November, New Zealand Q3 labour on 4 November, Australian trade on 5 November, the New Zealand election on 7 November, the GDT on 17 November, the Australian Wage Price Index and New Zealand trade on 18 November, and Australian October CPI on 25 November. Conviction is 3, not higher, because the score rests on one theme that is largely priced and both legs are heavily shorted, and not lower, because the calendar asymmetry is a fact rather than a forecast. The most important way this call could be wrong is a New Zealand unemployment rate at or below 5.3% on 4 November, which would revive December hike pricing and squeeze a crowded kiwi short. Where the chart sits against the call: we hold the stance as scored. Our reservation concerns entry, not direction. Spot sits at the 96th percentile of its 52-week closing range and at a 13-year high, after the largest daily move against the kiwi in nine years. Chasing the 28 October candle carries poor risk/reward, which is why the plan buys the retest of 1.2450-1.2490 rather than strength above 1.2540.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: On the two currency views, the Australian dollar ranks 5th of 11 tactically and the kiwi 10th of 11, so AUD/NZD pairs a mid-table currency against one of the weakest, and it is among the more attractive AUD crosses tactically. Among kiwi shorts, NZD/NOK and NZD/CAD express the oil terms-of-trade gap more directly, but AUD/NZD is the cleanest expression of the rate-divergence theme and has lower volatility. Among Australian dollar longs it offers less carry than AUD/CHF (460bp) or AUD/JPY (335bp) but much less exposure to global risk.

strategic.score_interpretation: A score of +0.1403 is Bullish, but only just, and it is sensitive to the weights. Policy (+0.1456) and Guidance (+0.0795) express the same view, that the RBNZ will deliver less than priced, while External Balance (-0.0848) is the one structural factor against the pair. At default weights the score would be +0.1036, barely above the Bullish threshold. That is why conviction is 2: the direction follows from the arithmetic, but the margin is thin. Mapping to conviction: a score at or above +0.10 maps mechanically to Bullish. Conviction 2 is the judgement attached to that stance.
strategic.rationale: Over the strategic horizon, Policy and Rates (0.28) and Guidance (0.15) together contribute +0.2251, against -0.0848 from External Balance (0.16), for a net of +0.1403, Bullish. The two currency views interact more awkwardly here. The kiwi-side view is Bearish on the RBNZ track undershooting pricing, which supports the pair. The Australian-side view expects the RBA to peak at 4.85% and shift to a neutral bias by February, with iron ore drifting to $82-90 a tonne, which works against it. The Australian-side view also favours shorting AUD/NZD, but its argument rests partly on the cross's position in its range and on a December RBNZ hike that is already about 76% priced, and a priced hike is not a surprise. What is priced is meaningful convergence: the 2-year spread of about 113bp sits well below the 185bp policy gap. We expect less convergence, with the gap at 160bp after a December RBNZ hike and 135-160bp into early 2027, because the RBNZ majority is cautious and StoneX judged that markets may still overestimate New Zealand tightening even after the hold. That is the edge. Against it, Australia's iron ore loss is structural, while New Zealand's oil-driven loss should partly unwind as a backwardated Brent curve and firmer dairy prices feed through. The path of least resistance is a carry-supported grind higher, tested at each scheduled decision. The key dates are the RBA on 8 December, the RBNZ decision and Monetary Policy Statement on 9 December, alongside the FOMC, Australian Q3 balance of payments on 1 December and GDP on 2 December, Australian December-quarter CPI on 27 January, the RBA on 9 February and the RBNZ Monetary Policy Review on 10 February. Conviction is 2 because the score sits close to the threshold and two of its three contributors share one forecast. A 9 December RBNZ track at or above market pricing, or an early RBA pivot as Australian unemployment rises toward 5%, would remove the case. Our view of the strategic score: we accept the strategic Bullish as scored, but it is more fragile than conviction 2 implies in one specific respect. Both positive contributors depend on the RBNZ under-delivering, while the one negative, Australia's terms of trade, compounds every month iron ore stays near $90. The variable we would watch most closely is the Australian October labour force in the third week of November. A fourth consecutive rise in unemployment would begin to narrow the gap from the Australian end before the RBNZ has published its track.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the Australian dollar ranks 7th of 11 and the kiwi 9th of 11 on the two currency views, so the gap between the legs narrows and AUD/NZD falls to a mid-ranked AUD cross. It remains more attractive than shorts in the kiwi crosses against low-yielders, NZD/CHF and NZD/JPY, but trails NZD/NOK and NZD/CAD as kiwi shorts while oil disruption persists. Among Australian dollar longs it ranks below AUD/CHF on carry, though its iron ore exposure is partly offset by the kiwi's own oil exposure.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish AUD/NZD (pair rising) over four weeks, conviction 3. No level is set here; price levels are set in the trade plan.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bullish AUD/NZD (pair rising) over one to three months, conviction 2, with a thin margin above the Bullish threshold.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Opposite to consensus in direction: located forecasts sit below the 1.24897 spot, implying a lower pair, while both our horizons are Bullish.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Directional rather than level-based: TD's 1.22 sits about 290 pips below the 1.24897 spot. A 10-provider aggregation of unnamed forecasters (not a bank view; ExchangeRates.org.uk, 14 October) puts Q4 2026 at 1.2142 (range 1.1905-1.2280), about 350 pips below spot, with a path of 1.2213 for March 2027 and 1.1902 for June 2027. Our levels are 1.2620 at four weeks, 1.2640 at three months and 1.2650 at six months, about 400 pips above TD's 1.22 and about 480 pips above the aggregate Q4 figure.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The located forecasts predate two shocks within 30 minutes of each other on 28 October: the RBNZ's 4-3 hold against heavy hike pricing, and Australia's 3.7% trimmed mean CPI, which pushed RBA November pricing toward 79-88%. Consensus assumes the RBNZ resuming hikes will narrow the gap. We agree it will resume, but a widely expected December hike is not a surprise. A divided committee whose majority stresses weak household demand is likelier to publish a track below pricing on 9 December than above it. We also weigh the timing asymmetry and the New Zealand election tail, which appears in no located forecast, more heavily than consensus does. Where consensus is stronger is the Australian terms of trade and labour market, which we score against the pair under External Balance. BofA's call was made in August and its premise has since been overtaken: its economists had expected no change in Australian rates until mid-2027, with cuts from August 2027, but the RBA has since hiked in September and is priced to hike again on 3 November. We accept that this bearish consensus is partly right on mechanism, since the RBNZ has delayed tightening rather than abandoned it. Our divergence is on timing and on the size of the RBNZ track, not on whether the RBNZ hikes.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A long position collects about 183bp a year of carry, roughly 19 pips a month, plus any repricing of RBNZ expectations lower after the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If consensus is right, the RBNZ track validates market pricing, or the RBA signals a peak as Australian unemployment rises, and crowded kiwi shorts cover. The gap would then narrow from both sides and the move would likely be fast, because the kiwi market is thinner.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Bullish on the same driver, RBA-RBNZ policy divergence, but strength fades with time. Tactically the calendar lets only the RBA act and puts the New Zealand election inside the window. Strategically the RBNZ resumes on 9 December, External Balance gains weight and turns against the pair on Australia's structural iron ore loss, and the score falls to just above the threshold.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The RBNZ decision and Monetary Policy Statement on 9 December. A track at or above market pricing would remove most of the strategic case; a track below pricing would confirm it. The RBA decision on 9 February is the second checkpoint, where an Australian shift to a neutral bias would work against the pair.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Hold the Bullish view with tactical conviction through the 3-7 November event cluster, sized for kiwi-short squeezes around New Zealand data. Reassess conviction after the 9 December RBNZ track rather than extending it on carry alone. In practice the tactical position (stop at 1.2330 on a daily close) should be run separately from the strategic one (stop at 1.2190 on a weekly close). A tactical stop-out on a strong New Zealand labour print does not by itself invalidate the strategic view, which turns on the 9 December track.

catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 4.85%, priced at roughly 79-88%, would widen the policy gap to 210bp with no RBNZ decision until 9 December. The residual upside comes from the unpriced share and from hawkish guidance; a hold would be a sharp negative for the pair. The published calendar flags no projection round for this decision.

After gains of 1.2% and 2.5% at the two October auctions, a third gain would support New Zealand's terms of trade and the Fonterra milk price, weighing on the pair. Peak-season New Zealand milk supply limits the upside, and a flat result would leave oil as the dominant terms-of-trade driver.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Q3 labour market (household labour force survey, labour cost index)
catalysts.rationale: This is the main risk to the tactical view. Unemployment at or below 5.3% would revive December RBNZ hike pricing above 85% and squeeze a crowded kiwi short, pushing the pair lower. A print of 5.5-5.8% would trim December pricing toward 60% or below and support the pair. Westpac expects 5.5%.

The Australian-side view expects a goods surplus below A$2bn after August's A$0.495bn, reflecting iron ore near two-year lows and a high fuel import bill. That would confirm Australia's terms-of-trade drag, the structural factor that works against the pair over the strategic horizon.

Polls project the coalition to 61 seats only if the overhang is small. A hung or delayed result, about 40% likely, would keep a risk premium on the kiwi until special votes are counted. A Labour-led government would bring more borrowing and a likely dual RBNZ mandate. Both outcomes weigh on the kiwi and lift the pair, while a clean coalition win would remove the premium.

Tests whether the October rally in whole milk powder holds into peak supply. A cumulative November gain above 5-6% would offset part of New Zealand's oil terms-of-trade loss and weigh on the pair; a reversal would leave the kiwi's external drag intact.

catalysts.event: Australian Wage Price Index (Q3) and New Zealand merchandise trade (October)
catalysts.rationale: Australian wages, expected at 0.8% q/q, test whether second-round effects justify the RBA holding high; a 1.0% print would support the pair. New Zealand's October trade includes a roughly 15% rise in Brent, and another deficit near NZ$2bn would confirm the kiwi's oil drag. The Australian October labour force follows later that week.

catalysts.event: Australian Labour Force, October (week of 16 November; exact date approximate)
catalysts.rationale: After three consecutive rises to 4.7% and a 39,300 fall in September employment, a fourth rise to 4.9% or higher would start pricing an RBA peak and narrow the expected gap from the Australian end, the main strategic risk to the pair. A print of 4.6% or lower would extend the RBA's room to hold 4.85% and support the pair. The mid-October labour release was the session that pulled AUD/NZD sharply lower, which shows how sensitive the cross is to this print.

A trimmed mean at 3.8% or higher would make a further RBA hike live and widen expected policy divergence, lifting the pair. A reading of 3.4% or lower would cement an Australian peak at 4.85% and bring forward the narrowing of the gap from the Australian side.

catalysts.event: New Zealand official election result after special votes (late November; exact date approximate)
catalysts.rationale: Special votes typically move a seat or two, which decides an overhang-dependent result. A confirmed coalition removes the election premium on the kiwi and weighs on the pair. A Labour-led bloc reliant on Te Pati Maori adds to the premium and lifts the pair.

With iron ore below $95 and Brent above $100 for most of the quarter, the Australian-side view expects another record current-account deficit above A$28bn. That would confirm the structural external drag that is the main strategic factor against the pair, against New Zealand's smaller deficit.

A hold is the base case after a November hike. Any signal of further tightening would widen expected divergence the day before the RBNZ decides, while an explicit peak signal would begin narrowing the gap from the Australian side.

catalysts.event: RBNZ OCR decision with Monetary Policy Statement (same day as the FOMC)
catalysts.rationale: This is the strategic inflection point. A hike to 3.00% is about 76% priced, so the hike itself is not the signal; the published OCR track is. A track peaking at 3.25-3.50%, below market pricing, would support the pair despite the hike. A track at or above 3.75% would remove most of the strategic case.

catalysts.event: Australian CPI, December quarter (with trimmed mean)
catalysts.rationale: The December-quarter trimmed mean is the main input to the RBA's February decision. A reading of 3.8% or more would extend the Australian cycle and support the pair. A reading of 3.4-3.6% would support a shift to a neutral bias and narrow expected divergence.

The Australian-side view expects a hold at 4.85% and a shift to a neutral bias here, which would work against the pair. Because it comes a day before the RBNZ Review, its tone sets the relative-policy frame that New Zealand then responds to.

catalysts.event: RBNZ OCR decision with Monetary Policy Review
catalysts.rationale: Tests whether the RBNZ follows its December track with a second hike to 3.25%. Delivery in line with a modest track keeps the gap near 160bp; a faster pace narrows it and weighs on the pair, especially if the RBA has turned neutral the day before.

A new OCR track and forecasts. This is where we expect the market's 3.75-4.0% peak pricing to converge toward the RBNZ's 3.25-3.50%. Convergence from above supports the pair. A track lifted on a December-quarter core re-acceleration would narrow the gap.

The last scheduled RBA decision inside the strategic window. A 5.10% hike, a 35% probability on the Australian-side view, would extend the gap to the upside scenario. A hold with a neutral bias would leave carry as the only support.

assumptions: The price analysis uses daily closing prices, with intraday highs and lows, for 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 1.24897 at the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November falls on a Sunday, so the two-day gap covers a weekend with no missed trading session, and every level, pip distance and percentage in this report is anchored to that close. Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. They, the 200-week average and its slope, and the support zones are computed over the full weekday history from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30: 4,920 daily sessions, 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly observations. No weekend sessions were present or removed. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days.

Data quality: no resistance zone met the two-touch threshold, while nine support zones did. With the pair at its highest since 2013 there are no historical swing closes above spot, so resistance is drawn from round numbers, the observed 14 and 28 October highs and the rectangle's measured move, each labelled as having zero computed touches. The 10-year yields supplied with the price data are September monthly averages (Australia 5.283%, New Zealand 4.94%) and are quoted only as monthly figures; live comparisons use daily closes of 5.137% (30 October) and 4.90% (29 October).

Implied volatility for AUD/NZD is an estimate, not a quote, because no option is listed on the cross. It combines listed AUD/USD and NZD/USD at-the-money options observed 29 October with a realised correlation of 0.627, and the three-month figure is measured at 98.7 days. The method has run low by roughly 9-18% where it could be checked, so 6.716% is treated as a floor, the bias-adjusted range is stated alongside it, and the carry-to-vol ratio of 0.27 is a ceiling. No AUD CFTC percentile and no implied-vol percentile were provided in the report, so those fields are null.

Carry and forward points use the CME AUD/NZD futures calendar spread (December 2026 to March 2027), -182.6bp annualised, observed 29 October, treated as what a long position earns (+183bp). That figure combines the interest differential with any cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve, so it is not reported as the policy differential (185bp).

Factor stances, confidences, weights and the weighted scores are this analysis's own and are reproduced as scored. They were set on fundamental evidence (rates, data, central bank communication, positioning, trade and cross-asset), and the pair's recent trading was deliberately excluded from every factor except Market Structure. The chart informs only entries, targets, stops, sizing, scenarios and the technical narrative. Where it suggests a different lean, as on Factor 9, that is stated as commentary and the score is left unchanged.

Weight adjustments raise Policy and Guidance and lower Risk Appetite and USD Liquidity. At default weights the scores would be +0.1954 tactically and +0.1036 strategically, so both stances survive without the adjustments.

Bilateral goods trade is IMF Direction of Trade Statistics for 2024. CFTC positioning is for the week to 27 October 2026, and no series exists for the cross. Kiwi percentiles and open interest are flagged estimates. Bank-dividend flows from New Zealand to Australia are described qualitatively from one July 2026 commentary. The catalyst dates for the Australian October labour force (week of 16 November) and the New Zealand special-vote result (late November) are approximate, as the report gives only the week or month.

Bank consensus for this cross is thin. TD Securities and BofA are the only named bank forecasts located, and BofA's dates from August. The 10-provider aggregation does not name its providers, and NAB's January projections are stale and unweighted. Retail and statistical-model forecast sites were not used.
Scenario probabilities, targets, entries and stops are our own. Scenario targets are measured from the 1.24897 spot, and expected values are shown both before and after carry.
